content: Hi, thanks so much for taking the time to chat today. I'm looking forward to hearing about the University of Puget Sound Courseware System and how it can better support your educational practices. The way this will go is pretty simple: I'll ask you some questions, but feel free to pause or ask me to clarify anything at any point. To get started, could you describe the project context and the problem the system should address from your perspective?

Right now, course information is spread across a few different tools and a lot of manual communication, which makes it harder for students and faculty to stay organized. We want one online place where courses, assignments, materials, discussions, and grades can be managed more consistently and accessed easily. The main problem is reducing friction in day-to-day teaching and learning while giving us a system that can grow and be refined as we understand the needs better.

Thanks for that overview. Could you share some specific examples or situations where the current spread-out tools and manual communication cause the most friction for students or faculty? What does that look like in practice?

A common issue is when a professor updates an assignment in email or on a class site, but not everyone sees it right away, so students miss deadlines or use the wrong instructions. Another example is course materials being posted in different places, so students have to check multiple systems just to find readings, slides, or the discussion board. For faculty, it creates extra work because they end up repeating announcements and manually tracking submissions or grades instead of having everything in one place.

That makes a lot of sense—having everything scattered definitely adds overhead. To help us design the right system, could you share any assumptions or expectations you have about the environment where this courseware will be used? For example, what kinds of devices or internet access do students and faculty typically have, or are there existing systems it needs to integrate with?

We should assume students and faculty will use it from laptops most of the time, but it also needs to work reasonably well on phones and tablets for quick checks. Internet access is generally available, but people do use it from off campus and in less-than-ideal conditions, so it should be dependable and not too heavy. I know it will need to fit with university login and probably some existing student information systems, but the exact integration points I’d need to verify with IT.

Thanks for sharing those details about device use and integration. To help us understand the impact this system should have, could you describe what measurable outcomes or improvements the university hopes to see once the courseware is in place? For example, are there specific goals around student engagement, faculty workload, or administrative efficiency that you’d like to track?

We’d want to see fewer missed assignments and fewer complaints about not being able to find course information, since that’s a sign the system is doing its job. For faculty, a meaningful improvement would be less time spent on repetitive communication and manual grade tracking. On the administrative side, we’d like smoother course setup and fewer support issues, but I don’t think we’ve defined formal metrics yet, so that would need to be worked out.

That’s helpful to understand the kinds of improvements you want. How do you imagine the university would track or measure these outcomes over time to know the system is working well? Are there particular indicators or reports that would be useful?

I think usage reports would be important, like how often students and faculty are logging in, accessing materials, submitting work, and participating in discussions. We’d also want to look at support tickets and complaints to see whether the same problems are coming up less often after adoption. Beyond that, grade-related outcomes might be discussed, but I’d be cautious about tying too much directly to the courseware without more context.

I appreciate your insights on tracking usage and support issues. Shifting gears a bit, could you share some of the specific terms or language that professors, students, and administrators commonly use when talking about courses, assignments, or grading at the university? Understanding this kind of domain terminology will help us make sure the system speaks the same language as its users.

People usually talk about things in pretty standard academic terms like courses, sections, assignments, readings, syllabi, discussions, and grades. Faculty may refer to office hours, due dates, grading rubrics, and course announcements, while administrators talk more about enrollment, rosters, and term setup. Students usually just want clear labels for what they need to do next, so consistency and familiar wording matter a lot.

Are there any terms or phrases related to courses, assignments, or grading that tend to cause confusion or are understood differently by professors, students, or administrators? How should the system handle those to keep things clear for everyone?

Yes, some terms can mean different things depending on who is using them, especially things like “section,” “assignment,” or “final grade” versus an informal progress mark. Faculty may also use department-specific language that students won’t immediately recognize. The system should keep labels simple and consistent, and where a term might be ambiguous, it should use brief explanations or context rather than assuming everyone interprets it the same way.

Are there any current methods or tools the university uses to help clarify or explain ambiguous terms to students and faculty? For example, do professors provide glossaries, or are there preferred ways the system should offer explanations or help to keep everyone on the same page?

Some professors do their own thing, like putting definitions in the syllabus or explaining terms in class, but there isn’t one consistent university-wide method that I’m aware of. I think the system should probably help with simple inline explanations or hover text for confusing labels, plus a help area that students can check without having to ask someone. If we can make the language clearer in the interface itself, that would probably reduce the need for extra glossaries.

You mentioned the importance of clear and consistent language in the system interface. How consistent is the use of academic terms like "assignments," "sections," or "grades" across different departments or user roles? Are there any notable variations or local jargon that the system should accommodate or perhaps help standardize?

The core terms are fairly consistent across the university, but departments do sometimes add their own jargon around course activities or grading practices. For example, one department may treat a project or lab differently from a standard assignment, even though students just see it as work to submit. I’d lean toward standardizing the main system terms and allowing departments to add a little local description where needed instead of changing the core language too much.

That makes a lot of sense to standardize core terms while allowing some local descriptions. Thinking about the system’s features, what kinds of tools or functions do you imagine the courseware should include to help manage or present these local variations and standard terms clearly? For example, should there be ways for departments to add descriptions or notes that students and faculty can easily see? How might that work in practice?

Yes, I think departments should be able to add short explanatory notes or custom descriptions in places where their terminology differs from the default. Those notes should show up right where the term appears, rather than being buried somewhere else, so students and faculty can understand the meaning in context. It would also help if the system kept the standard term visible and only supplemented it with the local explanation, so things stay consistent across courses.

That sounds very helpful for clarity. How do you envision departments managing or approving these local descriptions? Should there be a review process or permissions to keep things consistent and up to date?

Yes, I’d expect some kind of permission control, probably with a few designated department editors rather than every instructor changing the wording independently. A light review step would make sense for shared descriptions so the language stays accurate and doesn’t drift over time. I’m not sure whether that review should be formal or just an approval by the department chair or coordinator, but it should definitely not be completely open-ended.

Thanks for explaining the approach to managing local descriptions. Shifting a bit, are there other important business rules or policies the courseware system should enforce? For example, rules around assignment submissions, grading practices, access permissions, or anything else that might affect how the system behaves or what it allows users to do?

Yes, there are definitely some important rules around who can see and do what. Students should only access the courses they’re enrolled in, and professors should only manage their own course sections unless they’ve been given some special role. For assignments and grades, the system should respect due dates and grade visibility rules, and it should be clear when something is locked, late, or still hidden from students.

You mentioned the importance of showing when assignments or grades are locked, late, or hidden. Could you walk me through how the system should behave or present information differently in these various states? For example, what should students or professors see or be able to do when something is late versus locked or still hidden?

If something is late, students should still be able to submit it if the instructor allows late submissions, but it should be clearly marked as late and maybe flagged for the professor. If it’s locked, the student should see that they can’t submit or open it yet, and the system should explain why, like an upcoming release date. If grades are hidden, students should know the grade exists in the system but not see the score or feedback until the professor releases it.

You’ve given a great overview of how the system should handle normal states like late submissions or locked assignments. I’m curious—how should the system handle exceptions or unusual cases where standard workflows don’t quite fit? For example, interdisciplinary courses, experimental grading methods, or special departmental practices that might not follow typical rules. How flexible should the system be in accommodating those?

It should be flexible enough to handle exceptions, but not so flexible that every course becomes its own custom system. Interdisciplinary courses may need shared access for multiple instructors, and some departments may use pass/fail, contract grading, or other special grading setups that should be supported without a workaround. My preference would be to have standard defaults with a controlled way to override specific rules when a department can justify it.

That makes a lot of sense to have standard defaults with controlled overrides. To get a clearer picture, could you share what kinds of exception or edge-case behaviors the system should be prepared to handle? For example, how should it manage things like late submissions beyond normal rules, grade disputes, or changes in enrollment status during a term?

The system should definitely handle enrollment changes during the term, because students do add and drop classes after things have already started. If someone is added late, they should gain access based on the current course dates, and if someone drops, their access should be removed promptly, though instructors may still need to keep the record for grading history. For grade disputes, I’d expect the system to preserve submission timestamps, grade changes, and comments so there’s a clear audit trail if a question comes up later.

You’ve shared great details about enrollment changes and grade dispute tracking. I’m curious, in these exception cases—like late submissions allowed beyond normal deadlines, or students added mid-term—how should the system handle notifications or alerts? For example, should students or professors get automatic reminders or flags, and how visible or persistent should those be?

Yes, automatic notifications would be important, especially for instructors when a late submission comes in, a student is added to a class late, or something is waiting on approval. Students should get clear reminders about deadlines and any changes that affect their access, but I wouldn’t want the system to overwhelm people with too many alerts. I’d expect the most important flags to stay visible in the course area until they’re resolved, while less urgent reminders could go through email or the dashboard.

That makes a lot of sense about balancing important notifications without overwhelming users. Shifting gears a bit, could you describe the key business data entities the courseware system must manage? For example, how should courses, assignments, submissions, grades, and users be structured and related within the system to best support your needs?

At a minimum, the system needs users, courses, enrollments, assignments, submissions, grades, and course materials. A course would be tied to one or more instructors and many students through enrollment records, and assignments would belong to a course and have due dates, release settings, and grading rules. Submissions should link a student to an assignment, and grades should link back to the submission or assignment with the ability to store comments and revision history.

Thanks for outlining those core entities so clearly. To build on that, could you describe what key data fields or attributes the system should store for each of these entities? For example, what details are essential for courses, assignments, submissions, or grades to support your workflows effectively?

For courses, we’d need things like course code, title, section, term, instructor, meeting details, and status. For assignments, the important fields are title, description, due date, release date, late policy, point value, and whether it’s visible to students. Submissions should store the student, timestamp, file or text content, late indicator, and any resubmission history, while grades should keep the score, rubric or feedback comments, who entered it, and when it was released.

You’ve provided a clear picture of the key data fields for courses, assignments, submissions, and grades. Building on that, how should the system handle the lifecycle of this data? For example, what should happen to submissions and grades if a student drops a course mid-term, or if an assignment is revised after students have already submitted work? How do you envision managing these kinds of changes while keeping data integrity and auditability?

If a student drops a course, their submissions and grades should not disappear, because instructors may still need them for audit and final grading records. The student should lose active access, but the historical record should remain tied to the course enrollment status at the time. If an assignment is revised after submissions already exist, the system should preserve the original version and create a new version so it’s clear which instructions each submission was made against.

Thanks for clarifying how the system should handle data lifecycle and versioning. Shifting gears a bit, could you describe what external systems the courseware system must interface with? For example, the university login system, student information system, or any other platforms. What key integration points and data flows do you expect between these systems and the courseware?

It definitely needs to connect to the university login system for single sign-on, so users can use their campus credentials. It should also integrate with the student information system for course rosters, enrollment changes, and basic course metadata like term and section. Beyond that, I’d expect some connection to university email or notification services, and possibly a file storage or document service, but I’m not sure yet whether those should be native or external integrations.

You mentioned integration with the university login and student information systems, plus possible links to email and file storage services. Could you walk me through how you envision these integrations working in practice? For example, what data flows or synchronization should happen automatically, and are there any timing or security considerations we should keep in mind for these external connections?

The login system should be real-time, so when someone signs in, the courseware verifies their campus identity right away. The student information system should sync rosters and enrollment changes automatically, probably on a scheduled basis with some near-real-time updates during registration periods, because that’s when changes matter most. For security, I’d expect encrypted connections, role-based access, and only the minimum data needed moving between systems, especially for grades and student records.

You’ve given a great overview of integration and security considerations. Shifting focus a bit, are there any legal, regulatory, or university standards—like data privacy laws, accessibility requirements, or academic integrity policies—that the courseware system must comply with? How do you see these shaping the system’s design and operations?

Yes, definitely. It needs to comply with student privacy rules, especially around grades and enrollment data, and it should meet accessibility expectations so students with disabilities can use it effectively. Academic integrity policies also matter, so the system should support things like plagiarism review workflows, audit trails for grade changes, and clear records of who accessed or modified course data.

You mentioned important compliance areas like student privacy, accessibility, and academic integrity. Could you share more about any specific university policies or legal standards—such as FERPA or ADA requirements—that the system must explicitly support? Also, how should these shape features like data access controls, audit logging, or user notifications within the courseware?

FERPA is the big one for student records, so access to grades, submissions, and roster data should be tightly limited to the right instructor, student, or administrator. ADA and general accessibility standards mean the interface has to work with screen readers, keyboard navigation, captions where needed, and accessible documents whenever possible. For audit logging, we’d want a record of who viewed or changed sensitive data and when, and for notifications, we should be careful not to expose private details in email or alerts beyond what’s necessary.

You’ve outlined important compliance needs well. To build on that, what are your expectations for the system’s security and privacy protections in practice? For example, how should the system enforce access controls day-to-day, handle sensitive student data securely, and manage these protections across integrations with other university systems?

Day to day, access should be role-based and course-based, so people only see the classes and records they’re actually tied to. Sensitive data like grades, submission contents, and personal student information should be encrypted in transit and protected at rest, with strong password or single sign-on authentication through the university. Across integrations, we’d want the same level of control and logging, so any data exchange with the SIS or email systems is traceable and limited to what each system truly needs.

You’ve given a solid overview of security and privacy protections. Building on that, how do you envision the system managing notifications and alerts—like those for late submissions, enrollment changes, or approval workflows—in a way that keeps critical information visible and actionable without overwhelming users with too many messages or flags?

I’d expect notifications to be configurable by role, so students get deadline and enrollment updates, while instructors get things like late submissions, missing work, and approval requests. The system should group routine messages and avoid repeated alerts for the same event, but anything time-sensitive or requiring action should stand out clearly in the courseware dashboard and maybe by email. It would also help if users could set some preferences, as long as we still deliver required notices.

Thanks for sharing your thoughts on notifications—that really helps clarify how to keep users informed without overload. Shifting gears a bit, what specific usability features or design principles do you think are most important to support the diverse users of this courseware system? For example, what would make the system easier or harder to use for students, faculty, or administrators, especially those who might be less tech-savvy or have accessibility needs?

Simplicity and consistency are probably the most important things. Students and faculty should be able to find courses, assignments, grades, and messages without hunting through too many menus, and administrators need clear workflows so routine tasks don’t require training every time. It would be harder to use if the terminology is inconsistent, pages are cluttered, or important actions are buried, especially for users who rely on keyboard navigation or screen readers.

You’ve highlighted the importance of simplicity and consistency nicely. Building on that, could you describe how easy you expect it to be for students and faculty to navigate the system and complete their key tasks—like finding and accessing assignments, submitting their work, and viewing grades? What would make those tasks smooth or frustrating in your view?

Those tasks should be very straightforward, with course materials, assignments, submission links, and grades all easy to reach from the main course page. It feels smooth when a student can get to an assignment in just a click or two, submit work without extra steps, and immediately see confirmation and any feedback. It becomes frustrating if there are too many nested pages, unclear labels, or if the system doesn’t clearly show whether something was submitted successfully or when grades were updated.

You’ve given a great picture of usability for regular users. Building on that, how important is learnability for new or occasional users—like first-time students or adjunct faculty? What kinds of onboarding, training, or embedded help features do you think would best support them in getting up to speed quickly?

Learnability is very important, especially for first-time students and faculty who only teach occasionally. I’d want the system to have clear first-time guidance, short tooltips or help text right where people need it, and maybe a simple walkthrough for common tasks like uploading an assignment or posting grades. A searchable help center and a few quick training materials would help too, because people usually want answers without having to sit through long training sessions.

Since the system will be used on laptops, phones, and tablets, sometimes over unreliable networks, how do you expect it to perform in those varied conditions? Are there particular performance or responsiveness features that would be especially important to keep the experience smooth for all users?

It should feel fast enough on a normal campus connection, but it also needs to stay usable on slower or spotty networks, especially for mobile users. Pages should load quickly, forms should save work reliably, and students shouldn’t lose a draft if the connection drops while they’re submitting something. I’d also expect it to work well on smaller screens without forcing a lot of zooming or side-scrolling.

You’ve given a great overview of general performance needs. Could you describe more specifically how quickly the system should respond when users access assignments, submit their work, or view grades? For example, what would feel fast enough or frustratingly slow, especially when using different devices or working off-campus on slower connections?

For everyday actions like opening an assignment or viewing grades, I’d expect the system to respond almost immediately, maybe within a second or two at most on a normal connection. Submitting work can take a little longer because files have to upload, but it should still give clear progress feedback and not leave people wondering if it worked. If it regularly takes more than a few seconds for simple page loads, that would start to feel slow, especially on phones or off-campus connections.

You’ve given a clear picture of how fast the system should respond under normal conditions. Thinking about those times when network connections are spotty or users are on phones or tablets with smaller screens, how do you expect the system to behave? For example, what features or design choices would help keep the experience smooth and prevent frustration in those less-than-ideal situations?

It should degrade gracefully, so if the network is weak the user still sees what’s been saved and what’s pending instead of just spinning or failing silently. Autosave, clear retry options, and a visible upload status would help a lot, especially for submissions or discussion posts. On smaller screens, the layout should stay simple and responsive, with the main actions easy to tap and important information not buried.

You’ve shared great details about handling weaker networks and smaller screens. To build on that, could you describe your expectations for how quickly the system should load and respond when users access assignments, submit their work, or view grades? Especially thinking about different devices like laptops versus phones, or when users are off-campus with slower connections—what would feel fast and reassuring versus frustrating or too slow in those scenarios?

On a laptop with a decent connection, opening an assignment or grades page should feel nearly instant, and anything beyond a couple of seconds starts to feel sluggish. On a phone or off-campus, I’d still want the core pages to load in a reasonable time, but the key thing is that the system shows progress, keeps the user from losing work, and confirms what happened as soon as possible. Submission is the most sensitive case, so even if the upload takes a bit longer, it needs to be very clear that the file is still going through and whether it succeeded.

You’ve given a clear picture of how the system should perform day-to-day. Shifting gears a bit, how do you expect the system to handle peak times—like the start of a term or right before assignment deadlines? What capacity or performance features would be important to keep things running smoothly during those busy periods?

At peak times, it should still stay responsive enough that students can get in, submit work, and check grades without the system slowing to a crawl. I’d expect it to handle a lot of simultaneous logins and uploads gracefully, maybe by prioritizing critical actions like submissions over less urgent activity. It would also help if the system could show honest status information, so people know whether there’s a delay instead of assuming the site is broken.

That makes a lot of sense about handling peak loads smoothly. Looking ahead, how do you see the system scaling over time as more users, courses, or new features get added? Are there particular scalability concerns or approaches you think would be important to keep the system reliable and responsive in the long run?

It should be able to grow without forcing a major redesign every time enrollment or course volume increases. I’d want the system architecture to support adding more courses, more file storage, and maybe new tools later without performance dropping off sharply. The main concern is avoiding something that works for a small rollout but becomes slow or hard to maintain once the university depends on it campus-wide.

You’ve shared valuable thoughts on scalability and growth. To dive a bit deeper into operational quality, how do you expect the system to manage performance and capacity during peak usage times—like right before deadlines or the start of a term—especially when network conditions might be spotty or variable? Are there particular features or behaviors you’d want to see to keep things running smoothly and users informed?

During those peak times, I’d want the system to stay available and keep the most important actions moving, even if some nonessential things slow down a bit. Clear status messages, queued uploads, and automatic retries would help users feel confident that their work is being handled. If there is a slowdown or outage, it should say so plainly and avoid making people guess whether their submission went through.

Thanks for sharing your thoughts on performance and reliability. Shifting gears a bit, thinking about moving from the current tools to this new courseware system, what are your top priorities or concerns around product migration and data conversion? Are there particular types of data or workflows that you feel absolutely must be preserved carefully during the transition?

The biggest priority is not losing course content, assignment records, or student grades during the move. I’d also be very concerned about preserving instructor materials and any discussion history that people still rely on for the class. The transition needs to be careful enough that faculty and students can pick up where they left off without having to rebuild everything by hand.

That makes sense about preserving everything carefully. Could you share more about how you envision the migration process itself? For example, are there particular steps, timing, or fallback plans you’d want to see to make sure the transition goes smoothly for faculty and students?

I’d want the migration to happen in a controlled window, probably between terms or during a quieter period, so we’re not disrupting active classes. It would be important to test the migrated data with a pilot group first and have a rollback plan if something looks wrong. Faculty should also get a short overlap period where they can verify their courses and fix anything before everyone is fully switched over.

You mentioned the importance of preserving course content, assignments, and grades during migration, which is really crucial. Could you tell me more about the specific types of data or workflows that you feel absolutely must be preserved carefully during the data conversion itself? For example, are there particular formats, discussion histories, grading details, or other elements that you see as especially sensitive or complex to move over without loss or disruption?

The most sensitive pieces are grades, assignment submissions, and anything tied to deadlines or grading rules, because even a small mismatch there would cause real problems. Discussion threads should keep their authorship and timestamps, and uploaded files need to stay linked to the right course and assignment. If there are rubric-based or category-based grading workflows, those should be preserved too, since recreating them manually would be tedious and error-prone.

You’ve clearly outlined the critical data that needs careful handling during conversion. Looking at the technical side, what specific challenges or requirements do you anticipate when converting these data formats or structures from the current systems into the new courseware? Are there particular data types or histories that you expect might be especially tricky to convert accurately or completely?

The trickiest parts will probably be anything with relationships and history, like discussion threads, nested replies, submission versions, and grade records tied to changing assignment settings. File attachments and old content formats can also be messy if the current tools store them in inconsistent ways. I’d expect some cleanup or mapping rules to be needed so the new system doesn’t lose context or import broken records.

Given the complexities you mentioned with converting data and preserving relationships, how would you want the project team to validate that the migration and data conversion were successful before fully switching over to the new platform? What kinds of testing, review, or fallback plans would give you confidence that the release is smooth and reliable for both faculty and students?

I’d want a mix of automated checks and real human review. The automated side should verify counts, links, grades, attachments, and timestamps, while faculty and staff do spot checks on a sample of real courses to make sure the content looks and behaves right. If anything fails those checks, we should be able to delay the cutover and keep the old system available until it’s fixed.

You’ve given a great overview of migration validation. Shifting a bit, have you noticed or do you anticipate any requirement conflicts or trade-offs in this project? For example, tensions between making the system highly flexible versus keeping it standardized, or between strong security and ease of use? I’d love to hear how you see those balancing out.

Yes, I’d expect some tension between flexibility and consistency. Faculty will want to organize courses in ways that fit their teaching style, but the university still needs a standard structure so support and training stay manageable. I also think there’s a trade-off between strong security and convenience, especially for things like access to course materials and grades, but in that case I’d lean toward security as long as it doesn’t make routine use painfully difficult.
